hints: Use the bromine test result to decide if A is saturated or unsaturated, then combine with the formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$ and the word unbranched.
walkthrough:
Link the test to the homologous series**
Think with me. Not decolourising bromine means no $\text{C=C}$ is present. With formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$ this fits the alkane general formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$. So A is a saturated alkane.

Draw the unbranched skeleton**
Unbranched means a continuous chain of 4 carbons. In skeletal form you draw a zigzag with 3 line segments and 4 vertices, each vertex is a $\text{CH}_3$ or $\text{CH}_2$ group. That is n-butane.
Final answer: A is unbranched butane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, drawn as a skeletal zigzag of 4 carbons.

hints: Recall what intermolecular force acts between non-polar alkane molecules and whether covalent bonds break on boiling.
Compare the shape and surface contact of a straight chain with a branched, more spherical isomer.
walkthrough:
Be clear what boiling breaks**
When an alkane boils you do not break $\text{C-C}$ or $\text{C-H}$ covalent bonds. You only separate whole molecules, so you only overcome weak induced dipole-dipole (London dispersion) forces between molecules.

Compare the shapes**
Picture unbranched butane as a long zigzag that can lie close to its neighbour along its whole length. Picture the branched isomer 2-methylpropane as more compact and spherical. The straight chain has a bigger surface area and many more points of contact.

Link contact to energy**
More contact allows stronger temporary dipoles to form between molecules, so London forces are stronger in A. More thermal energy is needed to pull the molecules apart, giving A the higher boiling point.

Final answer: Unbranched A has stronger induced dipole-dipole (London dispersion) forces.
Unbranched A has larger surface area / more points of contact, so more energy is needed to separate molecules.

hints: Use the formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$, the positive bromine test, and the need for geometrical isomerism to place the double bond.
walkthrough:
Narrow down the alkene**
Decolourising bromine tells you B is an alkene. Unbranched $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ gives only three possibilities: but-1-ene, but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene is branched so excluded. Only but-2-ene can show cis-trans isomerism, so B must be $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$ (but-2-ene).

hints: Think about what is special about rotation around a $\text{C=C}$ double bond compared with a $\text{C-C}$ single bond.
Look at the two groups attached to each carbon of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH}_3$ and check if they are the same or different.
walkthrough:
Why the double bond locks the shape**
A $\text{C=C}$ contains a pi bond formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals. Twisting would break that overlap, so rotation is restricted. The relative positions of groups are therefore fixed.

Why two different groups matter**
On the left carbon you have $\text{CH}_3$ and H, and on the right carbon you also have $\text{CH}_3$ and H. Because each double bond carbon has two different substituents, the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups can be locked on the same side (cis) or on opposite sides (trans). That is geometrical isomerism.

Final answer: There is restricted / no rotation about the $\text{C=C}$ double bond.
Each C of the $\text{C=C}$ carries two different groups, one $\text{CH}_3$ and one H.

hints: Start the mechanism from the electron rich $\text{C=C}$ and show how it attacks the nearest Br atom of $\text{Br}_2$.
Remember $\text{Br}_2$ must be shown polarised $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$-$\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ with an arrow in the $\text{Br-Br}$ bond.
Think about what positive intermediate forms on the alkene after one $\text{C-Br}$ bond is made.
Consider how the $\text{Br}^{-}$ ion formed uses its lone pair to complete the addition.
walkthrough:
Set up the first attack**
See the $\text{C=C}$ as a region of high electron density. It acts as a nucleophile. Draw a curly arrow starting in the middle of the $\text{C=C}$ bond and pointing to the nearer Br atom, which is $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$.

Break Br-Br correctly**
Show $\text{Br}_2$ as $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$-$\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ with the $\delta+$ end nearest the double bond. Draw a second curly arrow from the $\text{Br-Br}$ bond to the far $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ atom. This makes $\text{Br}^{-}$ and forms one $\text{C-Br}$ bond plus a carbocation on the other carbon.

Show the intermediate**
Draw the carbocation clearly with a positive charge on carbon, for example $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrC}^{+}\text{HCH}_3$. Accept a cyclic bromonium ion as an alternative. This is the key electrophilic addition intermediate.

Finish with bromide attack**
Now show $\text{Br}^{-}$ with its lone pairs and negative charge. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{Br}^{-}$ to the positively charged carbon to form the second $\text{C-Br}$ bond, giving $\text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCHBrCH}_3$.

Final answer: Electrophilic addition: curly arrow from $\text{C=C}$ to $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$ of polarised $\text{Br}^{\delta+}$-$\text{Br}^{\delta-}$; curly arrow from $\text{Br-Br}$ bond to $\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ to give $\text{Br}^{-}$; carbocation / bromonium intermediate formed; lone pair on $\text{Br}^{-}$ attacks carbocation carbon to give dibromoalkane.

hints: Think about how the high electron density of the approaching $\text{C=C}$ affects the electron cloud in the non-polar $\text{Br}_2$ molecule.
walkthrough:
See the repulsion effect**
As the electron rich double bond approaches $\text{Br}_2$, its pi electrons push the bonding electrons in $\text{Br}_2$ away. The nearer Br becomes $\delta+$ and the farther Br becomes $\delta-$. So the dipole is induced by the alkene itself.
Final answer: The high electron density / pi electrons of the $\text{C=C}$ repel electrons in $\text{Br}_2$ / induce a dipole in $\text{Br}_2$.

hints: Use the lack of colour change for C to decide its alcohol class among branched $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ isomers.
Use the orange to green change for D to decide its alcohol class and what type of product E must be.
Combine the fact that E has formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$ and liberates $\text{CO}_2$ from carbonate to identify its functional group and branching.
walkthrough:
Decode C**
No colour change with hot acidified dichromate means no oxidation. Among branched $\text{C}_4$ alcohols, only the tertiary alcohol resists oxidation. That is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{COH}$, where the C-OH carbon has no H to remove.

Decode D**
Orange to green means $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ is reduced, so D is oxidised. D is branched but must be primary or secondary. Under reflux a primary alcohol goes all the way to a carboxylic acid.

Build E from D**
E has formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$ and gives $\text{CO}_2$ with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$, so E is a carboxylic acid. Keeping the same branched skeleton as D gives $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCO}_2\text{H}$. Therefore D must be its parent alcohol $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{OH}$.

Final answer: C = 2-methylpropan-2-ol, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{COH}$.
D = 2-methylpropan-1-ol, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{OH}$.
E = 2-methylpropanoic acid, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{CHCO}_2\text{H}$.

hints: Write the general pattern acid plus carbonate gives salt plus water plus carbon dioxide, then insert E as $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$.
walkthrough:
Apply the acid carbonate pattern**
Carboxylic acids neutralise carbonate to give the sodium salt, water and carbon dioxide. Put 2 moles of acid to match $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$, giving $$2\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{C}_4\text{H}_7\text{O}_2\text{Na} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$$ Check atoms balance.

hints: Recall the name of the pale yellow solid with antiseptic smell formed in a positive iodoform test.
walkthrough:
Name the yellow solid**
A yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine is the classic positive test for a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ group. The solid is triiodomethane, $\text{CHI}_3$, commonly called iodoform.
Final answer: triiodomethane (iodoform), $\text{CHI}_3$.

hints: Use the orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH to establish the functional group present in both F and G.
Combine unbranched plus positive iodoform for F, and aldehyde plus chiral centre for G, to place the $\text{C=O}$ in each $\text{C}_5$ skeleton.
walkthrough:
Start from the carbonyl clue**
Both give an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, so both contain a $\text{C=O}$ group. They are either aldehydes or ketones with formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$.

Solve F**
F is unbranched and gives the iodoform reaction, so it must be a methyl ketone on a straight chain. The only fit is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$, pentan-2-one.

Solve G**
G gives a silver mirror with Tollens reagent, so it is an aldehyde. It is negative to iodoform and has a chiral centre. The branched aldehyde $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CHO}$ has a central carbon attached to H, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ and CHO, four different groups, so it is chiral. That is 2-methylbutanal.

Final answer: F = $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3$ (pentan-2-one).
G = $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CHO}$ (2-methylbutanal).

hints: Think about how many different groups must be attached to a single tetrahedral carbon to make it chiral.
walkthrough:
Picture the tetrahedron**
A chiral centre is a tetrahedral carbon bonded to four completely different groups, so its mirror image cannot be superimposed. In G the second carbon fits this exactly.
Final answer: A carbon / atom with four different groups / atoms attached.

hints: Look for the very broad absorption around 2500 to 3300 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ in H and the sharp carbonyl peak near 1700 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ in both spectra.
Notice that spectrum I has no broad O-H band but shows sharp C-H absorptions near 2900 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ plus a C=O peak.
walkthrough:
Read spectrum H**
See the very broad, deep valley from about 2500 to 3300 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. That breadth is characteristic of hydrogen bonded $\text{O-H}$ in a carboxylic acid. There is also a strong sharp dip near 1710 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ for $\text{C=O}$. So H shows $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{O-H}$.

Read spectrum I**
Spectrum I has no broad $\text{O-H}$ band. It shows sharp absorptions near 2900 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ for $\text{C-H}$ and a strong sharp dip near 1735 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ for $\text{C=O}$. So I shows $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-H}$.

Final answer: spectrum of H: $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{O-H}$.
spectrum of I: $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-H}$.

hints: Use the presence of O-H in H to decide between a carboxylic acid and an ester of formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2$.
Use the absence of O-H but presence of C=O in I to name the remaining ester isomer.
walkthrough:
Assign H**
Formula $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}_2$ with both $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{O-H}$ can only be a carboxylic acid. That is ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$.

Assign I**
With $\text{C=O}$ but no $\text{O-H}$, I cannot be an acid or alcohol. It must be the ester isomer, methyl methanoate, $\text{HCOOCH}_3$. This fits the $\text{C-H}$ and $\text{C=O}$ peaks and the molecular formula.

Final answer: H = ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2\text{H}$.
I = methyl methanoate, $\text{HCO}_2\text{CH}_3$.
